purpose: Answer the simple reader question in the title: how much money resident Indians sent abroad under RBI's Liberalised Remittance Scheme, and what the official purpose breakdown actually contains. Write like an editor who has read every cell and both footer notes in RBI Bulletin Table 36. Open with FY2025-26 at about $29 billion, roughly ₹2.56 lakh crore at that financial year's average exchange rate, below the FY2023-24 peak, and state immediately that LRS is not every dollar leaving India. Explain the 2015 reporting break before describing long-run growth. Walk through every top-level purpose, but organise the argument around findings rather than reciting ten labels. Surface six non-obvious results: Travel lost the top spot to Studies Abroad during the pandemic year; the monthly timing differs across all ten purposes; the five largest purposes formed 95% of the latest total; rising investment and property offset roughly one-third of declines elsewhere after the peak; the overall peak year is not every purpose's own peak; and equity or debt investment rose to become the third-largest latest purpose while deposits remained below their own peak. Hold two corrections at once: this is not a clean capital-flight measure, because deposits, property and equity/debt investment were only about 14% of the latest total; and it is not a foreign-holiday bill, because RBI's only two detailed travel months put roughly 40% of Travel under education. Treat the workbook footer on Others as an editorial warning: journals, investment maintenance, student-loan repayments and credit-card payments do not form one coherent behaviour. Use Bureau of Immigration departures only as context, never as a per-trip denominator. End with a question-led methodology section that states the exact aggregation, unit conversion, dash treatment, coverage break, travel taxonomy and missing demographic fields. Never use an em dash. Never claim a causal effect from the October 2023 TCS timing.
tension: One RBI table is routinely made to tell two dramatic stories, rich Indians taking holidays and money fleeing the country. The table supports neither story cleanly. Its administrative categories mix family support, education, travel, asset purchases and residual credit-card or loan payments, and RBI changed what it counted in 2015 and how it split travel in 2026.
requiredConcepts: RBI recorded about $29.0 billion of LRS outward remittances in FY2025-26, compared with a peak of about $31.7 billion in FY2023-24. The total was therefore about 8.7% below the peak, not at a fresh record.
Travel was about $16.4 billion in FY2025-26, or 56.7% of the ten-purpose total. Call it the official Travel category, not holiday spending.
Maintenance of close relatives was about $3.5 billion, equity/debt investment about $2.7 billion, gifts about $2.6 billion and Studies Abroad about $2.3 billion in FY2025-26.

Deposits, purchases of immovable property and investment in equity/debt together were about $3.9 billion, or 13.6% of FY2025-26 LRS remittances. Describe this as the clearly asset-building subset, not an exhaustive legal capital-account total.

Travel was the largest purpose from FY2016-17 onward except in FY2020-21, when Studies Abroad briefly moved ahead. Use this pandemic exception to show that the categories respond differently to shocks.

Use the full April 2008 to April 2026 workbook span to show all ten top-level purposes at monthly frequency. Across 2,170 possible top-level cells, plot all 2,119 published numeric values and preserve 51 literal dashes as gaps. Give each small-multiple panel its own scale, state that panel heights cannot be compared, and use it to discuss timing rather than size.
The five largest FY2025-26 purposes formed about 95% of the total. Use this to explain concentration without dropping the five small categories.

Purposes that declined after the FY2023-24 peak lost about $4.2 billion in total, while equity/debt investment and property added about $1.4 billion. The rises offset roughly one-third of the declines, producing a net fall of about $2.8 billion.

From FY2023-24 to FY2025-26, Studies Abroad fell by about $1.2 billion, maintenance of relatives by about $1.1 billion, gifts by about $1.0 billion and Travel by about $0.6 billion. Equity/debt investment rose by about $1.1 billion and property purchases by about $0.3 billion. These are movements, not identified causes.

Compare FY2025-26 with each purpose's own maximum across all 17 complete fiscal years. Equity/debt investment and property are at records, Travel is at 96.7% of its record, Studies Abroad at 44.7%, and Others at 26.9%. This is a distance-from-peak comparison, not a causal or predictive claim.

Give the investment shift its own section. Equity or debt investment reached $2.65 billion in FY2025-26, up 56% in one year and 76% from FY2023-24, and moved from fifth to third among purposes. Property also reached a record, while deposits remained about one-quarter below their FY2022-23 peak. These are gross declared-purpose outflows, not investor counts, net acquisitions, portfolio values or proof of capital flight.

RBI publishes all five travel children only for March and April 2026 in this workbook. Across those two months, education-related travel was about 39.5% of Travel and Other travel about 58.1%; business, pilgrimage and medical travel together were about 2.4%. Never project this two-month mix over the full year or older history.

The newest RBI note distinguishes travelling abroad for education from buying an education service without travelling, which remains under Studies Abroad. The same distinction applies to travel for medical treatment versus remotely purchased medical services.

The workbook footer says Others includes journal subscriptions, maintenance of investments abroad, student-loan repayments and credit-card payments. This is a heterogeneous residual and cannot support a single behavioural explanation.

The raw workbook unit is US dollar crore. Divide each raw value by 100 to store US dollar billion. The headline total is the sum of the ten top-level purpose columns only; the five travel children are nested and must never be added again.

Parenthetical rupee equivalents are approximate and use the average monthly INR-per-US-dollar rate over the corresponding financial year. They are context, not transaction-level rupee totals; keep the RBI source values and chart axes in US dollars.

Literal dashes are stored as null. Sparse top-level dashes contribute no published amount to the reconciled total, while the long run of dashes in the five travel-child columns means RBI did not publish that breakdown before March 2026.

From May 26, 2015, RBI brought private and business travel and several other current-account facilities under the common LRS ceiling, while setting the annual limit at $250,000 per resident individual. The post-2015 jump is partly a coverage change, so no clean CAGR should cross that break.

Indian-national departures rose much more slowly than LRS Travel remittances over the common 2016-2024 window. This establishes that departure counts alone do not explain the money series; it does not create a valid spending-per-trip estimate.

For most LRS purposes other than education or medical treatment, the TCS rate above the then Rs 7 lakh threshold rose from 5% to 20% from October 1, 2023. TCS is collected at source and generally creditable; timing around the change is not proof that it caused remittances to fall.

The table is an administrative measurement of gross outward flows by resident individuals. It has no remitter count, household income, state, age, destination, recipient, refund or return-flow field. Do not describe the average Indian, the average household, the destination of the money or permanent capital loss.
requiredSections: Is the latest LRS total a new record?

styleExample:
## What does RBI's Travel category actually contain?

Travel sounds precise until the table opens it up. In the two months where RBI supplies the full split, education takes a large slice. The residual called Other travel is broad too: holidays sit beside some international credit-card settlements. So the safe sentence is narrower than the tempting one. Travel is the largest official purpose. The data does not say all of it paid for holidays.
